claims.text: Hot-press sintering a thin, pure hafnium coating onto zirconium-alloy cladding will create a controlled, diffusion-bonded, graded Hf-Zr transition layer.
The Hf-Zr transition layer will provide robust adhesion between the hafnium coating and zirconium substrate.
At high temperature, hafnium will diffuse into the zirconium substrate.
Hafnium diffusion will form or further develop a graded Hf-Zr interface.
The graded Hf-Zr interface will evolve during oxidation to produce an HfO2-rich oxide scale.
The resulting HfO2-rich scale will be dense and protective.
The HfO2-rich scale will impede oxygen ingress into the cladding.
Impeded oxygen ingress will reduce oxidation of the underlying zirconium-alloy cladding.
Hafnium-coated cladding will have a significantly lower oxidation rate than uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding at approximately 1600 °C for up to 5 hours in air.
Hafnium-coated cladding will exhibit reduced oxidation-related weight gain relative to uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding under the stated conditions.
The hafnium-coated cladding will maintain its mechanical properties during service conditions.
The hafnium-coated cladding will maintain its thermal properties during service conditions.
Uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding has higher oxidation rates and weight gain than the proposed coated cladding under comparable high-temperature conditions.
The effectiveness of the coating depends on maintaining a precisely controlled hafnium diffusion depth.
An inadequate diffusion depth may provide insufficient oxidation protection.
Deviation from the required diffusion depth may degrade mechanical performance.
Oxidation in air at approximately 1600 °C for up to 5 hours simulates reactor accident conditions relevant to zirconium-alloy cladding.
